mainTopic: ברכות on seeing crowds, sages and kings, with stories about בן זומא, רב ששת and רבי שילא on gratitude and on earthly kingship as a reflection of heavenly kingship.
overview: The amud opens with רבי ירמיה בן אלעזר: ruined בבל harmed its neighbors, but ruined שומרון became vineyards that helped them. רב המנונא and a ברייתא then teach that one who sees 600,000 Jews says 'ברוך חכם הרזים', because ה׳ knows every distinct mind and face. בן זומא, seeing such a crowd on הר הבית, also thanked ה׳ for all the people whose work brings him ready-made bread and clothing, and he contrasts a grateful guest with an ungrateful one. After defining an אוכלוסא as at least 600,000 people, the גמרא lists ברכות for seeing sages and kings, both Jewish and non-Jewish. רבי יוחנן urges people to go greet kings. The blind רב ששת shows a skeptic that the king arrives in silence, like ה׳'s revelation to אליהו. רבי שילא, reported for judging without royal permission, is saved and given authority to judge. He then explains the verse 'לך ה' הגדולה' phrase by phrase, ending with the idea that even a minor leader is appointed from heaven. A ברייתא gives רבי עקיבא's different reading of the same verse.

steps.title: Two cursed places: בבל hurts its neighbors, שומרון helps them
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה בן אלעזר states that when בבל was cursed its neighbors were cursed too, but when שומרון was cursed its neighbors were blessed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה בן אלעזר said: When בבל was cursed, its neighbors were cursed. When שומרון was cursed, its neighbors were blessed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a short teaching that compares what happened to the neighbors of two destroyed places, בבל and שומרון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both places received a קללה, but the effect on the surrounding area was opposite. The ruins of בבל spread harm to the area around it. The ruins of שומרון became useful to the people around it.

keyTerms.meaning: Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar said:
When Babylonia was cursed, its neighbors were cursed.
When Samaria was cursed, its neighbors were blessed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opening statement of this passage; it continues the surrounding discussion of בבל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The destruction of בבל harmed its neighbors, while the destruction of שומרון benefited its neighbors.

steps.title: Verse proving בבל's ruin harmed its neighbors
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא repeats the first half of the teaching and proves it from ישעיהו: בבל will become a home for the קיפוד and swamps.
steps.simpleTranslation: When בבל was cursed its neighbors were cursed, as it is written: 'I will make it a possession for the bittern, and pools of water.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the source for the claim about בבל. It repeats the line and attaches a פסוק to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says ruined בבל will turn into marshland full of wild creatures. That kind of land is not just empty. It spreads damage and danger to the surrounding area, which is why the neighbors suffer too.

phrases.english: When Babylonia was cursed, its neighbors were cursed,
as it is written: 'I will make it a possession for the bittern'
'and pools of water.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides the scriptural source for the first half of step 1.
steps.raayaObject: That the curse of בבל spread to its neighbors.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ישעיהו יד:כג: 'וְשַׂמְתִּיהָ לְמוֹרַשׁ קִפֹּד וְאַגְמֵי מָיִם'

steps.title: Verse proving שומרון's ruin helped its neighbors
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proves the second half from מיכה: שומרון will become a field for planting vineyards.
steps.simpleTranslation: When שומרון was cursed its neighbors were blessed, as it is written: 'I will make שומרון a heap in the field, a place for planting vineyards, etc.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the source for the claim about שומרון, again repeating the line and attaching a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruined city becomes farmland for vineyards. Its neighbors gain productive land, so even the destruction turns into a benefit for them.

keyTerms.meaning: a heap of ruins in the field

steps.whatToRemember: Two cities were both cursed, but the outcomes differed. Ruined בבל became a swamp that hurt its neighbors. Ruined שומרון became vineyards that helped its neighbors.

phrases.english: When Samaria was cursed, its neighbors were blessed,
as it is written: 'I will make Samaria a heap in the field'
'for planting vineyards, etc.'

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב: ״וְשַׂמְתִּי שֹׁמְרוֹן לְעִי הַשָּׂדֶה לְמַטָּעֵי כָרֶם וְגוֹ׳״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallel to step 2; proves the second half of step 1.
steps.raayaObject: That the curse of שומרון brought blessing to its neighbors.
steps.raayaSupportSource: מיכה א:ו: 'וְשַׂמְתִּי שֹׁמְרוֹן לְעִי הַשָּׂדֶה לְמַטָּעֵי כָרֶם'

steps.title: Blessing on seeing huge crowds of Jews or of non-Jews
steps.stepSummary: רב המנונא rules that one who sees huge crowds of Jews says 'ברוך חכם הרזים'. On huge crowds of גוים, one says the פסוק 'בושה אמכם'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב המנונא said: One who sees multitudes of Israel says: 'Blessed… Who knows secrets.' On multitudes of gentiles he says: 'Your mother shall be ashamed, etc.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic: what a person says when he sees an enormous crowd of people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two different responses are given. For a vast crowd of Jews (understood as 600,000), one says a ברכה praising ה׳ as the 'Knower of secrets.' For a vast crowd of גוים, one says a פסוק from ירמיהו about the shame of a hostile nation.
steps.confusionAlert: 'אוכלוסי' does not mean just any group of people. The גמרא itself defines it later (step 16) as a crowd of at least 600,000.

phrases.english: And Rav Hamnuna said:
One who sees multitudes of Israel says:
'Blessed… Who knows all secrets.'
On multitudes of gentiles, he says:
'Your mother shall be ashamed, etc.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from the aggadic contrast of cities to a halachic rule about ברכות on seeing crowds.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: On a vast crowd of Jews one says 'ברוך חכם הרזים'; on a vast crowd of גוים one says 'בושה אמכם'.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the halachic ברכה of חכם הרזים, recorded in the שולחן ערוך.

steps.title: ברייתא explains why the blessing is 'Who knows secrets'
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches the same ברכה and gives the reason: no two people's minds or faces are alike, yet ה׳ knows each one.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: One who sees multitudes of Israel says: 'Blessed… Who knows secrets,' because their minds are not alike and their faces are not alike.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that matches רב המנונא's ruling and adds the reason behind the wording of the ברכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason is that each person in the crowd thinks differently and looks different. Only ה׳ knows the hidden thoughts of every single one. That is why He is praised as 'Knower of secrets.'

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
One who sees multitudes of Israel says:
'Blessed… Who knows all secrets'
because their minds are not similar to one another,
and their faces are not similar to one another.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב המנונא's ruling and explains the wording of the ברכה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ברכה is 'חכם הרזים' because ה׳ knows the distinct mind of every person in the crowd.

steps.title: בן זומא sees a crowd on הר הבית and adds a second blessing
steps.stepSummary: בן זומא saw a huge crowd from a step on הר הבית. He said 'חכם הרזים' and also 'Blessed is He Who created all these to serve me.'
steps.simpleTranslation: בן זומא saw a crowd on a step on הר הבית and said: 'Blessed… Who knows secrets,' and 'Blessed… Who created all these to serve me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא tells a story about בן זומא, who added a personal ברכה of thanks when he saw a giant crowd.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Besides the standard ברכה, בן זומא thanked ה׳ that all these people exist 'to serve me.' This sounds surprising, and it sets up the next lines, where he explains what he meant.
steps.confusionAlert: 'To serve me' is not arrogance. As the next lines show, it is gratitude: everyone's work benefits him.

phrases.english: Ben Zoma saw a crowd
from atop a step on the Temple Mount,
he said: 'Blessed… Who knows all secrets'
'and Blessed… Who created all these to serve me.'

steps.triggerLanguage: בֶּן זוֹמָא רָאָה אוּכְלוּסָא עַל גַּב מַעֲלָה בְּהַר הַבַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a story applying the ברכה, with an added personal ברכה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בן זומא said both חכם הרזים and 'שברא כל אלו לשמשני' on seeing a vast crowd.

steps.title: בן זומא explains: אדם הראשון worked hard for bread, I find it ready
steps.stepSummary: בן זומא explains his ברכה. אדם הראשון had to do every step of making bread himself, while he wakes up and finds bread ready.
steps.simpleTranslation: He used to say: How much effort did אדם הראשון exert before he found bread to eat! He plowed, sowed, reaped, bundled, threshed, winnowed, sorted, ground, sifted, kneaded, baked, and only then ate. And I wake up and find all this prepared for me.
steps.whatsHappening: בן זומא begins explaining what he meant by 'all these were created to serve me,' starting with bread.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He lists the many stages of making bread to show how much work one person alone would need. Because society divides the work among many people, he gets the finished product without effort. That is why a crowd is a reason to thank ה׳.

phrases.english: He used to say:
How many labors did Adam the first man toil
until he found bread to eat:
he plowed, sowed, reaped, and gathered sheaves,
threshed, winnowed, sorted, and ground,
sifted, kneaded, and baked,
and only afterward he ate.
And I wake up and find
all of these prepared before me.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר: כַּמָּה יְגִיעוֹת יָגַע אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the meaning of 'שברא כל אלו לשמשני' from step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Thanks to the work of many people, one enjoys bread without doing all its labors himself.
steps.whyThisMatters: Many of the stages listed here match the מלאכות of שבת (סדר הפת), a connection learners will recognize later.

steps.title: Same point with clothing: אדם הראשון worked hard, I find garments ready
steps.stepSummary: בן זומא makes the same point with clothing. אדם הראשון sheared, laundered, combed, spun, and wove before he had a garment, but he finds clothes ready.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how many labors did אדם הראשון exert until he found a garment to wear! He sheared, laundered, combed, spun, wove, and then found a garment. And I wake up and find all these prepared for me.
steps.whatsHappening: בן זומא gives a second example, clothing, to strengthen his point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The structure is the same as the bread example: a long list of steps, then 'and I wake up and find it ready.' Adding a second basic need shows that almost everything we have comes from other people's work.

phrases.english: And how many labors did Adam the first man toil
until he found a garment to wear:
he sheared, laundered, combed, spun, and wove,
and only afterward found a garment to wear,
and I wake up and find
all of these prepared before me.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכַמָּה יְגִיעוֹת יָגַע אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן עַד שֶׁמָּצָא בֶּגֶד לִלְבּוֹשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallel second example reinforcing step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Clothing, like bread, comes to a person ready-made through the labor of many others.

steps.title: All nations come to my door: the summary of בן זומא's gratitude
steps.stepSummary: בן זומא sums up: people of all nations eagerly come to his doorstep, and he wakes up to find everything before him.
steps.simpleTranslation: All nations eagerly come to the entrance of my house, and I wake up and find all these before me.
steps.whatsHappening: בן זומא wraps up his explanation with a general statement: the whole world's merchants and workers bring their products to him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line generalizes from bread and clothing to everything. Merchants and craftsmen from everywhere come to his door. So seeing a vast crowd reminds him that all these people's work serves him, and that is the reason for his ברכה 'שברא כל אלו לשמשני'.
steps.whatToRemember: On seeing a vast crowd of Jews, one says 'ברוך חכם הרזים', because ה׳ knows each person's unique mind and face. בן זומא added a ברכה of gratitude, because the labor of countless people provides him with bread, clothing, and everything else.

phrases.english: All nations diligently hurry
and come to the entrance of my house,

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲנִי מַשְׁכִּים וּמוֹצֵא כׇּל אֵלּוּ לְפָנַי.
phrases.english: and I wake up and find all of these before me.

steps.triggerLanguage: כׇּל אוּמּוֹת שׁוֹקְדוֹת וּבָאוֹת לְפֶתַח בֵּיתִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Generalizes the bread and clothing examples into a summary statement.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The whole world's labor reaches a person ready-made, so a vast crowd calls for gratitude to ה׳, Who 'created all these to serve me.'

steps.title: What a good guest says
steps.stepSummary: בן זומא describes a guest who notices and appreciates the host’s work.
steps.simpleTranslation: He would say: What does a good guest say? The host went to so much trouble for me. He brought me meat, wine, and loaves. Everything he did was for me.
steps.whatsHappening: בן זומא gives the good guest’s way of speaking about a meal. The guest focuses on how much the host did for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The guest lists concrete things the host provided. Saying it was all “for me” expresses gratitude, rather than a claim that no one else benefited.

phrases.english: He would say:
What does a good guest say?

phrases.aramaic: כַּמָּה טְרָחוֹת טָרַח בַּעַל הַבַּיִת בִּשְׁבִילִי,
phrases.english: How much effort the host went to for me!
How much meat he brought before me!
How much wine he brought before me!
How many loaves he brought before me!
And all the effort he went to—
he went to only for me.

steps.triggerLanguage: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר: אוֹרֵחַ טוֹב מַהוּ אוֹמֵר?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: בן זומא moves from appreciating the work that supplies his own needs to appreciating a host’s work.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A good guest speaks appreciatively about the host’s efforts.

steps.title: What a bad guest says
steps.stepSummary: בן זומא contrasts the good guest with one who dismisses the host’s effort.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what does a bad guest say? What trouble did this host take? I ate one piece of bread and one piece of meat, and drank one cup. Whatever he did was only for his wife and children.
steps.whatsHappening: בן זומא now gives the opposite response to the same kind of hospitality. This guest minimizes both what he received and the host’s intention to help him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The contrast is about how the guest chooses to view the host’s work. The bad guest counts only his own small portion and credits the rest of the work to the host’s family.

phrases.english: But what does a bad guest say?

phrases.aramaic: מַה טּוֹרַח טָרַח בַּעַל הַבַּיִת זֶה?
phrases.english: What effort did this host go to?
I ate one piece of bread,
I ate one piece,
I drank one cup.

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל טוֹרַח שֶׁטָּרַח בַּעַל הַבַּיִת זֶה —
phrases.english: All the effort this host went to—

phrases.aramaic: לֹא טָרַח אֶלָּא בִּשְׁבִיל אִשְׁתּוֹ וּבָנָיו.
phrases.english: he went to only for his wife and children.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It presents the opposite way a guest can describe the host’s work.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A bad guest dismisses the host’s efforts instead of acknowledging them.

steps.title: Verses for the two kinds of guest
steps.stepSummary: The teaching connects the good guest and bad guest to two verses.
steps.simpleTranslation: About the good guest, what does the verse say? “Remember that you magnify his work, which people have praised.” About the bad guest it is written: “Therefore people fear him, etc.”
steps.whatsHappening: The teaching now attaches verses to the two descriptions of guests. The first verse speaks of praising someone’s work; the second is cited for the bad guest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first verse fits the guest who makes the host’s effort visible. The second is introduced as a contrast, without a further explanation of its wording here.

phrases.english: About a good guest, what does [the verse] say?
“Remember that you magnify his work,
which people have praised.”
About a bad guest it is written:
“Therefore people fear him, etc.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It supplies verses after the two contrasting descriptions.
steps.raayaObject: The contrast between acknowledging another person’s work and failing to do so.
steps.whatToRemember: The good guest notices the host’s work; the bad guest talks it down.

steps.title: A verse introduces a new discussion of crowds
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a verse about a man who came among people, preparing to identify him.
steps.simpleTranslation: “And the man, in the days of שאול, was old and came among men.”
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא leaves the guest example and quotes a verse to set up its next move. The next statement will explain whom the verse describes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words about coming among people connect this verse to the earlier discussion of a great crowd. The verse is the starting point; its interpretation comes next.

phrases.english: “And the man, in the days of Saul,
was old and came among men.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It ends the guest discussion and sets up another statement about crowds.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A verse about coming among people is introduced for interpretation.

steps.title: The verse refers to ישי
steps.stepSummary: An attributed teaching identifies the man as יִשַׁי and describes him moving and teaching among large crowds.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said—and some say רב זביד, and some say רב אושעיא—that this is ישי, father of דוד: he went out with a multitude, entered with a multitude, and taught in a multitude.
steps.whatsHappening: The teaching identifies the man in the verse as יִשַׁי, father of דָּוִד. It then explains his connection to crowds through three activities.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The three examples give content to the verse’s description of him among people. The גמרא preserves different reports of which sage gave this interpretation.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רָבָא, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַב זְבִיד, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַב אוֹשַׁעְיָא:
phrases.english: Rava said—and some say Rav Zevid, and some say Rav Oshaya:
This is Yishai, father of David,
who went out with a multitude,
entered with a multitude,
and taught in a multitude.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַב זְבִיד, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַב אוֹשַׁעְיָא:
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It interprets the verse just quoted.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The verse describes יִשַׁי as going, coming, and teaching among a multitude.

steps.title: A multitude of this kind is not found in בבל
steps.stepSummary: עוּלָּא states a received teaching about the absence of an אוּכְלוּסָא in בָּבֶל.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said: We have a received teaching that there is no multitude in בבל.
steps.whatsHappening: עוּלָּא adds a statement about where an אוּכְלוּסָא is found. The following teaching will help clarify how large that term means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This does not mean that בָּבֶל has no crowds at all. It refers to an אוּכְלוּסָא in the special sense under discussion.

keyTerms.meaning: we have received as a teaching

phrases.english: Ulla said: We have received a teaching
that there is no multitude in Babylonia.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It adds a geographic statement about the kind of multitude just mentioned.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: עוּלָּא says an אוּכְלוּסָא is not found in בָּבֶל.

steps.title: How large a multitude must be
steps.stepSummary: A teaching gives the minimum size of an אוּכְלוּסָא.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: A multitude is no fewer than six hundred thousand.
steps.whatsHappening: A teaching now puts a number on the term אוּכְלוּסָא. It means at least six hundred thousand people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains why an ordinary large gathering need not count as an אוּכְלוּסָא. It also clarifies the scale of עוּלָּא’s preceding statement.

phrases.english: It was taught: A multitude is not fewer
than six hundred thousand.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא: אֵין אוּכְלוּסָא פְּחוּתָה מִשִּׁשִּׁים רִבּוֹא.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It supplies the size required by the term in the preceding statements.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An אוּכְלוּסָא has at least six hundred thousand people.
steps.whatToRemember: Here אוּכְלוּסָא means a crowd of at least six hundred thousand, not just any busy gathering.

steps.title: Blessings on seeing sages
steps.stepSummary: The sages teach different blessing words for seeing Jewish sages and sages of other nations.
steps.simpleTranslation: The sages taught: One who sees the sages of Israel says, “Blessed … Who has shared of His wisdom with those who revere Him.” For sages of the nations of the world, one says, “Blessed … Who has given of His wisdom to flesh and blood.”
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching lists blessings said when seeing sages. It gives one wording for חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל and another for חַכְמֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both blessings say that wisdom comes from ה׳. The wording changes from “shared” with “those who revere Him” to “given” to “flesh and blood.”

phrases.english: The sages taught: One who sees the sages of Israel
says, “Blessed … Who has shared of His wisdom with those who revere Him.”
For sages of the nations of the world, one says:
“Blessed … Who has given of His wisdom to flesh and blood.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The discussion moves from the size of a crowd to blessings said on seeing particular people.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Different blessing wordings are given for seeing חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל and חַכְמֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם.

steps.title: Blessings on seeing kings
steps.stepSummary: The same teaching gives parallel blessing words for seeing Jewish kings and kings of other nations.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who sees kings of Israel says, “Blessed … Who has shared of His glory with those who revere Him.” For kings of the nations of the world, one says, “Blessed … Who has given of His glory to flesh and blood.”
steps.whatsHappening: The teaching continues with blessings for seeing kings. It keeps the two different wordings but now speaks about glory rather than wisdom.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pattern matches the preceding blessings for sages. The change from wisdom to glory fits the change from sages to kings.

phrases.english: One who sees kings of Israel says:
“Blessed … Who has shared of His glory with those who revere Him.”
For kings of the nations of the world, one says:
“Blessed … Who has given of His glory to flesh and blood.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It applies the same two-part pattern of blessings to kings.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Different blessing wordings are given for seeing מַלְכֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל and מַלְכֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם.
steps.whatToRemember: For sages, the blessings mention wisdom; for kings, glory. Each pair distinguishes יִשְׂרָאֵל from the other nations.

steps.title: Make an effort to greet kings
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says to go greet both Jewish kings and kings of other nations.
steps.simpleTranslation: A person should make an effort to run to greet kings. Seeing kings of other nations may help a person later recognize the difference between them and Jewish kings.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds רבי יוחנן’s advice after the teachings about blessings for kings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The advice is not limited to Jewish kings. רבי יוחנן gives a reason for seeing other kings too: that experience can provide a point of comparison later.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
A person should always strive to run
to greet the kings of Israel.
And not only to greet the kings of Israel,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אֲפִילּוּ לִקְרַאת מַלְכֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם,
phrases.english: but even to greet kings of the nations of the world,
so that, if he merits it, he will distinguish

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין מַלְכֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לְמַלְכֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם.
phrases.english: between the kings of Israel and the kings of the nations of the world.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: לְעוֹלָם יִשְׁתַּדֵּל אָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from blessings said upon seeing kings to the value of going to greet them.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person should make an effort to greet both Jewish kings and kings of other nations.

steps.title: A blind sage goes to greet the king
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת joins the crowd, and a skeptic questions why he has come.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת was blind, but he went with everyone to greet the king. A skeptic mocked him, and רב ששת answered that he knew more than the skeptic did.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story illustrating the previous advice. It sets up a test: can רב ששת recognize the king’s arrival without seeing him?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The skeptic assumes that going to greet a king is pointless for someone who cannot see. רב ששת challenges that assumption, but has not yet shown how he knows.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet was blind.
Everyone was going
to greet the king,
and Rav Sheshet got up and went with them.
A certain skeptic encountered him and said to him:
Jugs go to the river; where do broken jugs go?
He said to him: Come and see
that I know more than you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Introduces a case of someone following the advice to greet a king.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The story presents רב ששת’s claim that he can know when the king arrives despite being blind.

steps.title: Two noisy troops pass without the king
steps.stepSummary: The skeptic mistakes the noise of two passing troops for the king’s arrival; רב ששת rejects both guesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: The first troop passed noisily, and the skeptic said the king was coming. רב ששת said no. The same exchange happened when the second troop passed.
steps.whatsHappening: The story tests the skeptic’s method twice. Each time, he treats a noisy troop as a sign that the king has arrived.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ששת rejects both guesses. The repeated mistake prepares us to notice a different sign when the third troop passes.

phrases.english: The first troop passed.
When it made noise,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא מִינָא: אֲתָא מַלְכָּא.
phrases.english: that skeptic said to him: The king has come.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: לָא קָאָתֵי.
phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said to him: He is not coming.
The second troop passed.
When it made noise,
that skeptic said to him:
Now the king is coming.
Rav Sheshet said to him:
The king is not coming.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins testing רב ששת’s claim against the skeptic’s guesses.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Noise from the first two troops does not mark the king’s arrival.

steps.title: The quiet troop signals the king
steps.stepSummary: When the third troop is quiet, רב ששת says the king is certainly arriving.
steps.simpleTranslation: The third troop passed. When it became quiet, רב ששת said: Certainly the king is coming now.
steps.whatsHappening: The story gives רב ששת’s answer to the test. He identifies quiet, rather than noise, as the sign of the king’s arrival.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This reverses the skeptic’s earlier guesses. The next question will ask רב ששת how he knew to use that sign.

phrases.english: The third passed.
When it became quiet,
Rav Sheshet said to him:
Certainly the king is coming now.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts the quiet third troop with the two noisy troops.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב ששת identifies the king’s arrival from the quiet.

steps.title: The skeptic asks how he knew
steps.stepSummary: The skeptic asks רב ששת for the basis of his prediction.
steps.simpleTranslation: The skeptic said to him: How do you know that?
steps.whatsHappening: The skeptic now asks רב ששת to explain his sign. This question sets up the source רב ששת will give next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The issue has shifted from whether רב ששת can see to how he interpreted the quiet. His answer will explain why he expected the king after it.

phrases.english: That skeptic said to him:
How do you know this?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא מִינָא: מְנָא לָךְ הָא?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Requests an explanation for רב ששת’s identification of the king’s arrival.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why did רב ששת take the quiet as the sign that the king was coming?

steps.title: He learns the sign from a verse
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת compares earthly kingship to heavenly kingship and quotes a verse in which the still, quiet sound follows wind, earthquake, and fire.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת says earthly kingship resembles heavenly kingship. He quotes a verse: after a powerful wind, an earthquake, and fire—none of which is identified as the place of God’s presence—comes a still, small voice.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת answers the skeptic by giving the source for his expectation of quiet. He quotes the verse’s sequence in full.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse places dramatic, noisy events before the still, small voice. רב ששת uses that pattern as an analogy for the king arriving after the noisy troops.

phrases.english: He said to him:
For earthly kingship is like heavenly kingship,
as it is written: “Go out and stand on the mountain
before the Lord, and behold, the Lord is passing by,
and a great and strong wind
splits mountains and breaks rocks
before the Lord; the Lord is not in the wind,
and after the wind, an earthquake;
the Lord is not in the earthquake.
And after the earthquake, a fire;
the Lord is not in the fire,
and after the fire, a still, small voice.”

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דְּמַלְכוּתָא דְאַרְעָא כְּעֵין מַלְכוּתָא דִרְקִיעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the skeptic’s request for רב ששת’s source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב ששת applies the verse’s movement from noise to quiet to the order of the king’s procession.

steps.title: He blesses when the king arrives
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת blesses the arriving king, and the skeptic mocks him for blessing someone he cannot see.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the king arrived, רב ששת began to bless him. The skeptic said: Are you blessing someone you do not see?
steps.whatsHappening: The king arrives, and רב ששת says a blessing. The skeptic raises one last objection based on רב ששת’s blindness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story has shown that רב ששת identified the king’s arrival. The skeptic now shifts to the act of blessing: he questions blessing a person whom רב ששת cannot see.

phrases.english: When the king came,

phrases.aramaic: פָּתַח רַב שֵׁשֶׁת וְקָא מְבָרֵךְ לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: Rav Sheshet began to bless him.
That skeptic said to him:

phrases.aramaic: לְמַאן דְּלָא חָזֵית לֵיהּ קָא מְבָרְכַתְּ?
phrases.english: Are you blessing someone whom you do not see?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the king’s arrival and moves from recognizing him to blessing him.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The story reports רב ששת blessing the king despite his blindness.

steps.title: What happened to the skeptic?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks about the skeptic’s fate.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what happened to that skeptic?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns from the exchange about the king to the skeptic’s fate. This question sets up two reported accounts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The text does not answer the skeptic’s last remark directly. Instead, it closes the story by asking what became of him.

phrases.english: And what happened to that skeptic?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from the skeptic’s remark to the end of his story.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What ultimately happened to the skeptic?

steps.title: One account says his eyes were gouged out
steps.stepSummary: The first reported account says the skeptic’s companions gouged out his eyes.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say that his companions gouged out his eyes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the first answer to its question about the skeptic. It identifies his companions as the ones who harmed him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is presented as one reported version, not as the only account. A different version follows immediately.

phrases.english: Some say:
His companions gouged out his eyes,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the first reported answer about the skeptic’s fate.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: According to the first account, the skeptic’s companions gouged out his eyes.

steps.title: Another account gives a different ending
steps.stepSummary: A second account says רב ששת directed his gaze at the skeptic, who became a pile of bones.
steps.simpleTranslation: Others say that רב ששת directed his eyes at the skeptic, and the skeptic became a pile of bones.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives an alternative ending to the story. This time it attributes the skeptic’s fate to רב ששת rather than to the skeptic’s companions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two accounts differ about what happened and who brought it about. The text leaves both versions in place.
steps.whatToRemember: The story begins with רב ששת going to greet a king, shows how he identifies the king’s arrival through quiet, and ends with two accounts of the skeptic’s fate.

phrases.english: And some say:
Rav Sheshet directed his eyes at him,
and he became a pile of bones.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי: רַב שֵׁשֶׁת נָתַן עֵינָיו בּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides an alternative to the first account of the skeptic’s fate.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: According to the second account, רב ששת directed his gaze at the skeptic, who became a pile of bones.

steps.title: A flogging leads to a royal summons
steps.stepSummary: רבי שילא flogs a man, who reports him for judging without royal permission.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שילא had a man flogged for relations with a non-Jewish woman. The man reported him to the royal court, which sent a summons.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new story about רבי שילא. The man's complaint brings רבי שילא before the royal authorities.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The complaint is about רבי שילא exercising authority without the king's permission. That sets up the story's focus on who grants the power to judge.

phrases.english: Rabbi Sheila had that man flogged
who had relations with a non-Jewish woman.

phrases.aramaic: אֲזַל אֲכַל בֵּיהּ קוּרְצֵי בֵּי מַלְכָּא,
phrases.english: He went and informed on him at the royal court,
saying: There is a man among the Jews

phrases.aramaic: דְּקָא דָּיֵין דִּינָא בְּלָא הַרְמָנָא דְמַלְכָּא.
phrases.english: who judges cases without the king's authorization.
He sent a royal messenger for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story develops the earlier theme of earthly kingship.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The opening events establish the conflict over רבי שילא's authority to judge.

steps.title: The court asks for evidence
steps.stepSummary: רבי שילא gives the court a different description of the act, and אליהו appears as a witness.
steps.simpleTranslation: Asked why he flogged the man, רבי שילא says the man had relations with a female donkey. Asked for witnesses, he says yes; אליהו appears as a person and testifies.
steps.whatsHappening: The royal court questions רבי שילא about the flogging. His answer is followed by testimony from אליהו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The court first asks for a reason and then for evidence. The testimony lets its inquiry proceed on the description רבי שילא gave.

phrases.english: When he came, they said to him:
Why did you flog this man?
He said to them: Because he had relations with a female donkey.
They said to him: Do you have witnesses?
He said to them: Yes.
Elijah came and appeared to him as a person,
and testified.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא אָמְרִי לֵיהּ: מַאי טַעְמָא נַגֵּדְתֵּיהּ לְהַאי?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The summons becomes an inquiry into the flogging.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי שילא supplies a reason and, when asked, testimony appears.

steps.title: רבי שילא explains why he did not execute the man
steps.stepSummary: The court calls the man liable to death; רבי שילא says exile has left his community without authority to execute.
steps.simpleTranslation: The officials say that, if so, the man is liable to death. רבי שילא answers that since exile, they have had no authority to execute; the officials may do as they wish.
steps.whatsHappening: The court asks why the punishment stopped at flogging. רבי שילא answers by distinguishing its authority from his community's authority.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does not dispute the court's stated penalty here. He explains why he did not carry it out himself.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרִי לֵיהּ: אִי הָכִי, בַּר קְטָלָא הוּא!
phrases.english: They said to him: If so, he is liable to death!

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: אֲנַן מִיּוֹמָא דִּגְלֵינַן מֵאַרְעִין
phrases.english: He said to them: From the day we were exiled from our land,
we have no authority to execute.
You may do with him whatever you wish.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ: אֲנַן מִיּוֹמָא דִּגְלֵינַן מֵאַרְעִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The court draws a consequence from the testimony; רבי שילא explains his limited authority.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Since exile, they lack authority to execute, while the royal court can decide what to do.

steps.title: רבי שילא praises divine and earthly kingship
steps.stepSummary: While the court deliberates, רבי שילא quotes a verse and explains his words to the officials.
steps.simpleTranslation: As they examine the case, רבי שילא begins, “Yours, Lord, are the greatness and the power…” Asked what he said, he blesses God for granting earthly kingship and giving the officials authority and a love of justice.
steps.whatsHappening: While the officials consider the case, רבי שילא quotes a verse. When they ask what he said, he gives them an explanation about their authority.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His explanation connects earthly kingship to heavenly kingship. This also prepares the verse that he will interpret after the story.

phrases.english: While they examined his case,
Rabbi Sheila began and said:
“Yours, Lord, are the greatness and the power, etc.”
They said to him: What are you saying?
He said to them: This is what I am saying:
“Blessed is the Merciful One who gives kingship on earth
like kingship in heaven,
and gave you authority and a love of justice.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The court deliberates, and רבי שילא speaks about the authority it holds.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי שילא explains his words as praise for God, who grants earthly authority.

steps.title: The court gives רבי שילא authority to judge
steps.stepSummary: The officials welcome רבי שילא's respect for royal honor and hand him a staff.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say that royal honor is very dear to him. They give him a staff and tell him to judge.
steps.whatsHappening: The officials respond favorably to רבי שילא's words. Their response reverses the complaint that brought him before them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man accused רבי שילא of judging without royal permission. Now the officials explicitly tell him to judge.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ: חַבִּיבָא עֲלֵיהּ יְקָרָא דְמַלְכוּתָא כּוּלֵּי הַאי!
phrases.english: They said: The honor of royalty is so dear to him!
They gave him a staff
and said to him: Judge cases.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ: חַבִּיבָא עֲלֵיהּ יְקָרָא דְמַלְכוּתָא כּוּלֵּי הַאי!
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The officials act on their favorable understanding of רבי שילא's words.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The officials authorize רבי שילא to judge.

steps.title: The man challenges רבי שילא's account
steps.stepSummary: The man calls רבי שילא a liar; רבי שילא answers with a verse explaining his choice of words.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי שילא leaves, the man asks whether God works miracles for liars. רבי שילא calls him wicked and cites a verse that uses donkey imagery.
steps.whatsHappening: The man confronts רבי שילא outside the court. רבי שילא answers by pointing to the wording of a verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man is challenging the description רבי שילא gave the officials. רבי שילא's reply explains why he used the word “donkey”; the danger from that reply appears next.

phrases.english: As he was leaving,
that man said to him:
Does the Merciful One perform such a miracle for liars?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: רָשָׁע, לָאו חֲמָרֵי אִיקְּרוּ?
phrases.english: He said to him: Wicked man, are they not called donkeys?
As it is written: “Whose flesh is the flesh of donkeys.”

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הַהוּא גַּבְרָא: עָבֵיד רַחֲמָנָא נִיסָּא לְשַׁקָּרֵי הָכִי?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רבי שילא receives permission to judge, the original complainant challenges his account.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי שילא cites scriptural donkey imagery to explain his wording.

steps.title: רבי שילא sees an immediate threat
steps.stepSummary: רבי שילא believes the man is about to report his words and identifies him as a pursuer.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שילא sees that the man is going to tell the officials he called them donkeys. He calls the man a pursuer, invokes the rule of acting first against someone coming to kill you, and kills him with the staff.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא completes the confrontation. רבי שילא sees a danger in what the man is about to report and acts against him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The narrative presents רבי שילא's fear that a report to the authorities will put his life at risk. It gives that fear as the reason he invokes the rule about a pursuer.

keyTerms.meaning: a pursuer who poses a lethal threat

phrases.english: He saw that the man was going to tell them
that he had called them donkeys,
and said: This man is a pursuer.
And the Torah said: If someone comes to kill you,
— act first and kill him.
He struck him with the staff and killed him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבי שילא's explanation creates the risk that the man will report him again.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The story ends with רבי שילא treating the expected report as a threat to his life and killing the man.

steps.title: רבי שילא begins explaining the verse
steps.stepSummary: Because the quoted verse helped him, רבי שילא begins interpreting its words, starting with creation and the exodus.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שילא says that since a miracle happened for him with this verse, he will interpret it. He connects “the greatness” to creation and “the power” to the exodus from Egypt, citing a verse for each.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves from the story to רבי שילא's explanation of the verse he quoted in court. This opening sets up the phrase-by-phrase readings that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He assigns an event to each phrase and then cites wording from another verse. The first two connections are creation and the exodus.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר: הוֹאִיל וְאִתְעֲבִיד לִי נִיסָּא בְּהַאי קְרָא,
phrases.english: He said: Since a miracle happened for me through this verse,
I will interpret it:
“Yours, Lord, is the greatness” — this is the act of creation,

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן הוּא אוֹמֵר: ״עֹשֶׂה גְדֹלוֹת עַד אֵין חֵקֶר״.
phrases.english: and so it says: “He does great things beyond searching out.”
“And the power” — this is the exodus from Egypt,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וַיַּרְא יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת הַיָּד הַגְּדֹלָה וְגוֹ׳״.
phrases.english: as it says: “And Israel saw the great hand, etc.”

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר: הוֹאִיל וְאִתְעֲבִיד לִי נִיסָּא בְּהַאי קְרָא, דָּרֵישְׁנָא לֵיהּ:
steps.relationToPreviousStep: With the confrontation over, רבי שילא returns to the verse he used in court.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי שילא begins a phrase-by-phrase interpretation of the verse.

steps.title: The glory and the triumph
steps.stepSummary: רבי שילא connects two more phrases to the sun and moon for יהושע and to the fall of Rome.
steps.simpleTranslation: “The glory” refers to the sun and moon standing still for יהושע. “The triumph” refers to Rome's downfall. A verse follows each reading.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שילא continues through the next two phrases of the verse. He names an event for each and cites supporting wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sun-and-moon citation directly describes their stopping. For Rome's downfall, he cites a verse using the word “their triumph” or “their blood.”

phrases.english: “And the glory” — this is the sun and the moon
that stood still for Joshua,
as it says: “And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, etc.”
“And the triumph” — this is the downfall of Rome.

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן הוּא אוֹמֵר: ״וְיֵז נִצְחָם עַל בְּגָדַי וְגוֹ׳״.
phrases.english: And so it says: “Their blood spattered on My garments, etc.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The phrase-by-phrase interpretation continues.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי שילא links the next two phrases to the event of יהושע and to Rome's downfall.

steps.title: The ארנון and סיסרא wars
steps.stepSummary: Two further phrases are linked to the war at Arnon and the war against סיסרא.
steps.simpleTranslation: “The majesty” refers to the war of the Arnon valleys. “For all in heaven and on earth” refers to the war against סיסרא, when the stars fought from heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שילא gives two more readings of the verse. Each reading is followed by a citation about the war it names.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first citation names the wars of God. The second makes the phrase about heaven especially clear: it describes stars fighting from heaven.

phrases.english: “And the majesty” — this is the war of the Arnon valleys,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״עַל כֵּן יֵאָמַר בְּסֵפֶר מִלְחֲמֹת ה׳
phrases.english: as it says: “Therefore it is said in the book of the wars of the Lord,
Vahev in Sufa, etc.”

phrases.aramaic: ״כִּי כֹל בַּשָּׁמַיִם וּבָאָרֶץ״ — זוֹ מִלְחֶמֶת סִיסְרָא,
phrases.english: “For all in heaven and on earth” — this is the war against Sisera,
as it says: “From heaven the stars fought,
from their courses, etc.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבי שילא continues assigning events to successive words of the verse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The next phrases refer to the Arnon war and the war against סיסרא.

steps.title: The kingdom and the one exalted
steps.stepSummary: רבי שילא links the verse's next phrases to the wars of עמלק and גוג ומגוג.
steps.simpleTranslation: “Yours, Lord, is the kingdom” refers to the war against עמלק. “And the one exalted” refers to the war of גוג ומגוג. He quotes a verse for each.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שילא continues the same phrase-by-phrase reading. These two phrases are connected to two wars.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first citation speaks of the divine throne; the second addresses גוג as a prince. The sequence is moving toward its final phrase, “as head above all.”

phrases.english: “Yours, Lord, is the kingdom” — this is the war against Amalek,

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן הוּא אוֹמֵר: ״כִּי יָד עַל כֵּס יָהּ״.
phrases.english: and so it says: “For a hand is upon the throne of the Lord.”
“And the one exalted” — this is the war of Gog and Magog,
and so it says: “I am against you, Gog,
chief prince of Meshekh and Tubal.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The interpretation advances to the verse's phrases about kingship and exaltation.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי שילא identifies the two phrases with the wars of עמלק and גוג ומגוג.

steps.title: Even a small appointment comes from heaven
steps.stepSummary: רב חנן בר רבא quotes רבי יוחנן: even the head of a minor water-distribution group is appointed from heaven.
steps.simpleTranslation: On “as head above all,” רב חנן בר רבא says in the name of רבי יוחנן: Even the head of a group responsible for distributing water is appointed from heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: A new named teaching explains the verse's final phrase. It applies heavenly appointment even to a very small leadership position.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier story concerned permission to judge under an earthly king. This closing teaching states a broader point: appointments to authority, even modest ones, come from heaven.

keyTerms.meaning: a group associated with distributing water

steps.whatToRemember: The passage begins with a dispute over earthly permission to judge and ends by saying that even a small position of authority is appointed from heaven.

phrases.aramaic: ״לְכֹל לְרֹאשׁ״ — אָמַר רַב חָנָן בַּר רָבָא
phrases.english: “As head above all” — Rav Hanan bar Rava said
that Rabbi Yohanan said:
Even the head of a water-distribution group
is appointed from heaven.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״לְכֹל לְרֹאשׁ״ — אָמַר רַב חָנָן בַּר רָבָא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The reading of the verse reaches its final phrase and closes on the source of authority.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Even a minor leadership appointment is from heaven.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא's reading of the verse's five praises
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא in the name of רבי עקיבא links five words of the verse to קריעת ים סוף, מכת בכורות, מתן תורה, ירושלים, and the בית המקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא taught in the name of רבי עקיבא: "Yours, ה׳, is the greatness" refers to the splitting of the Red Sea. "And the power" refers to the plague of the firstborn. "And the glory" refers to the giving of the תורה. "And the triumph" refers to ירושלים. "And the majesty" refers to the בית המקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second way to read the same verse that רבי שילא was explaining. This time the source is a ברייתא in the name of רבי עקיבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שילא tied the verse's words mostly to wars and miracles across history. רבי עקיבא ties them to the founding moments of the Jewish people: two miracles of the Exodus, the giving of the תורה, and the holy places, ירושלים and the בית המקדש. The two readings do not argue about any law. They are simply two ways of explaining the same praises.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא (a teaching from the time of the משנה that is not in the משנה itself)
The splitting of the Red Sea
The giving of the תורה at Sinai
The triumph or eternity, which here refers to ירושלים
The majesty, which here refers to the בית המקדש

steps.whatToRemember: The verse ״לְךָ ה׳ הַגְּדֻלָּה...״ gets two readings. רבי שילא connects it to wars and historical events. רבי עקיבא connects it to the Exodus, מתן תורה, ירושלים, and the בית המקדש.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two readings. רבי שילא matched ״הַגְּדֻלָּה״ to creation, while רבי עקיבא matches the same word to קריעת ים סוף. They are separate, parallel interpretations, not one continuous list.

phrases.english: It was taught in a baraita in the name of Rabbi Akiva:
phrases.notes: Here the גמרא brings a different, earlier source for this teaching.

phrases.aramaic: ״לְךָ ה׳ הַגְּדֻלָּה״ — זוֹ קְרִיעַת יַם סוּף.
phrases.english: "Yours, O Lord, is the greatness": this is the splitting of the Red Sea.
"And the power": this is the plague of the firstborn.
"And the glory": this is the giving of the Torah.
"And the triumph": this is Jerusalem.
"And the majesty": this is the Temple.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the verse רבי שילא interpreted in steps 36 to 39 and offers a parallel interpretation from a ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי עקיבא interprets the five praises of the verse as referring to קריעת ים סוף, מכת בכורות, מתן תורה, ירושלים, and the בית המקדש.
